utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning. Like the last three days, we are sitting with two Judges only, pursuant to Rule 15 bis, due to the absence of Judge Nyambe. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I have some information for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. We have translations of the following documents, Mr. President: P1955, and we have the B/C/S translation; P1961, also the B/C/S translation; P2136, again the B/C/S translation; P2137, an English translation; and P2138 and P2139, B/C/S translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. They will no longer be marked for identification, pending translation, but received as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Please sit down. Good morning again. Welcome back to the courtroom. I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made at the beginning of your testimony still applies. Mr. Vanderpuye is putting questions to you during his re-examination. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, again. Good morning to everyone, and good morning to you, Colonel. I'm just going to put a few questions, maybe a little bit more than a few questions, to you concerning some issues that arose during your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You testified in this case that after General Tolimir told you that the preparations should be stopped concerning the prisoners, the 1300 prisoners that were expected at Batkovic, that you met with General Simic, and that's at page 12942 through 12943 of the transcript of these proceedings. You testified that he called Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic, and that's at the same page, transcript 12943, and that you relayed his order to Commander Vulin, Dragisa Vulin, to go to Zvornik to obtain some prisoners, and that's at the same page of the transcript, lines 17 through 20. And that's essentially what you say in your interview on pages 36 through 38 in the English and pages 34 through 36 in the B/C/S. And on Tuesday, referring to Colonel Pandurevic's 16 July interim combat report, and that was shown to you during your 2nd February interview, General Tolimir asked you the following; transcript page 13044, lines 18 through 24: "Q. If it had been the way Pandurevic stated in his report, if they had fought as a unit of the Zvornik Brigade," and he's talking about the East Bosnia Corps military police, "whom would have the authority over them?" And your answer, which followed at lines 25 on page 13044 through 13045, was: "No, because the military police, which was a part of the military police battalion that was deployed to Zvornik, was only sent there to carry out a specific task, namely to accept some of the prisoners of the BH Army taken prisoner and to conduct them to the Batkovic collection centre. That's a task he received from the battalion commander, and I only relayed it to him." Now, I want to show you P2183. That should be your statement from 2nd February 2010. And we'll need to go to page 83 in the English and page 73, into 74, in the B/C/S. When you were asked -- when you were shown the interim combat report of Vinko Pandurevic, you were asked the following question by Mr. Nicholls. He said, and I'll just read it - it starts at line 14: "One last thing. Sorry it's getting a bit late. This is a document I want to show you, just so you can see it and have a chance to read it and give any comment you may like to, and it's 0068-4874. It's an interim combat report from 16 July 1995, from Vinko Pandurevic, the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, to his command, the Drina Corps. And so this is after the fall of Srebrenica." And he says: "Anyway, I'll ask you to read it. The reason I'm giving it to you is because in paragraph 2 you can read the whole thing, but Pandurevic writes that part of the Military Police Platoon from the IBK," East Bosnia Corps, "are carrying out a decisive defence in the brigade zone, sealing off and searching the terrain and the wider areas, and that continues. So Vinko Pandurevic, in his report, is explaining that IBK military police --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have that document in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm reading from the interview at the moment, and I'll show the document in just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is that the right page in B/C/S on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We're going to have to flip over the page in B/C/S in just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Or I think we've reached that moment. We should flip it over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you see it on the screen, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It should be at the top, lines 1 through 7, Mr. President, in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And Mr. Nicholls says what the report says, and then he says: "So Vinko Pandurevic, in his report, is explaining that IBK military police are taking part in actions in Zvornik." And your answer is: "That's this part of the Military Police Platoon which went there because Zvornik Brigade blocked some prisoners." Now, you go on, if we go on to the next page in English -- we should be going to page 80 -- I'm sorry, we should go to page 85 in the English and page 74 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, it's becoming a very compound question, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm just putting this in context for the witness, Mr. President. I should -- I'll get to the point in just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to welcome all present. I wish for peace in this house, and may the proceedings today be according to God's will and not as I will. I would like for Mr. Vanderpuye to put questions based on the context, because neither I nor the witness are able to actually follow and refer to what he is citing. And also for a while there was no text on the monitors. So it could perhaps be put in a way that is easier for us to follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was exactly my comment as well. Would you be able to read from that part again which is on the B/C/S on top, because when you were reading that part, it was not on the screen at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have to go back, I think, to page 74 in the English to be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, page 83 in English, I think, is where I was. All right. At the top of the page in the B/C/S, this should correspond to the last sentence of the English, where Mr. Nicholls says "in the zone of the brigade," so he says -- it leads up by saying: "... The Military Police Platoon from the IBK are carrying out a decisive defence in the brigade's zone, sealing off and searching the terrain and the wider area, and that continues. "So Vinko Pandurevic, in his report, is explaining that IBK military police are taking part in actions in Zvornik." Your answer, in response to reading this document, is that: "That's this part of the Military Police Platoon which went there because the Zvornik Brigade blocked some prisoners." You then go on to say, and this is at page 85 in the English; and 74, lines 26 through 28, in the B/C/S: "I can guarantee, and you can check with the commander of the battalion and the commanding officer who went there, that this military police platoon from the IBK did not take part in combat activities. Pandurevic just wrote it."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye -- yes, we didn't have it in English on the screen. Now it is there, line 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness that 16 July interim combat report, and that's P1089.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I won't read it out, but take a look at paragraph 2 which was referred to you in your interview back in 2010, and let me know when you've had a chance to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could the B/C/S version be enlarged a bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you stand by what you said in your interview, that that is this part of the Military Police Platoon which was sent there after you spoke with General Simic and directed his order to Dragisa Vulin?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I stand by what I said, from what I've been following so far, and I'm saying that a part of the platoon that took part in the combat was duty-bound to inform me and the commander that they had participated in combat, that they had sustained casualties. But they reported back to us that they had carried out the assignment, which was to take custody, escort, and hand over the prisoners of war to the Batkovic Collection Centre. I do not really want to deal with the report and what the commander of the Zvornik Brigade wrote. That is up to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to show you 65 ter 7322, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, while the document is still here, perhaps we can see if the witness is correct. Perhaps he can be asked about the contents of item 3, where Colonel Pandurevic states that he had opened the corridor. You cannot conduct combat actions once the corridor is open. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's up to the Prosecutor to decide his way of conducting the interrogation of the witness during re-examination. I don't see that this was an objection to any question, but is a proposal, how to conduct the re-examination. It's up to Mr. Vanderpuye to do that. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I actually asked for 7332. I apologize if I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. It's 7332.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What we have on the screen in front of you, Colonel, is a combat readiness report dated 29 November 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have a partial translation of the document because we haven't had enough time between yesterday and today to complete it. But the relevant portions of it are translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you can see, sir, that this is from the Command of the 3rd Battalion of the Military Police, and it's dated 11 -- 29th November 1995. If we can go to the last page of this document. I don't think we have a translation of the last page, but if we go to the bottom, you can see that it's signed by Komandant Major Dragisa Vulin. That's the Command of the Military Police Battalion; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we go to page 3 in the B/C/S, we'll see item number 5. I'm mistaken, I'm sorry. Page 4 in the B/C/S, we'll see item 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And under item number 5, it provides information about military police tasks carried out by the Military Police Battalion, and it talks about the permanent tasks of providing security for the commander of the East Bosnia Corps, for the chief of the East Bosnia Corps; I believe it's probably the Chief of Staff. The chief of security of the East Bosnia Corps, that would be you; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And these are the types of things that you would see in a combat readiness report; an assessment of the activities of the unit during the period that it's covered; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We saw a report on combat readiness for 1995. We saw the first page, the last page, and then this page. However, the report has many more pages, it's more voluminous, about all the activities from command and control to logistics support or logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let's take a look at item number 2, which should be at page 3 in the B/C/S. In item number 2, it says: "Units dispatch to other fronts outside the area of responsibility of the East Bosnia Corps." And there it includes the following information; that: "The battalion was dispatched to the front in the zones of responsibility for the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps and the Drina Corps for 112 days or three and a half months." It reads also that: "All tasks were completed successfully; that the battalion was commanded by the Command of the 2nd Krajina Corps, the Command of the 1st Light Infantry Brigade of the East Bosnia Corps, and the 1st Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade, in which formations the battalion operated, and it shows the best that the battalion successfully completed its combat tasks." Now I want to show you item number 1, and that should be on page 1 of the B/C/S, and it comes under the heading of "Command and Control." If we go down to item letter K, it says, directly under item number 1: "Organisation, preparation, execution of the combat activities." In item number K, it says: "Blocking the breakthrough of the Srebrenica Muslims in the area of Baljkovica and Crni Vrh in the zone of the 1st Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade of the Drina Corps." And that's exactly what Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic's interim combat report states.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, was that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us about that? Can you explain it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-colonel, the commander of the Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade, Mr. Pandurevic, and Major Dragisa Vulin wrote that in their own characteristic way in the textual reports, Vinko Pandurevic for the daily combat report, and then they kind of embroidered their annual balance of work. So he used a little bit of a robust terminology for that task. I still am asserting, and, if necessary, the Prosecution or the Court can, if they deem it significant, check - Mr. Vulin is still accessible, available, and alive - it wasn't him who went, anyway. One of his senior officers actually went with some 10 or 15 policemen, with a truck, and over a period of a number of days they were taking custody and bringing over prisoners of war of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the Batkovic Camp, which is what we saw yesterday by looking at the list of captured members of the B&H Army. We saw that they were not all brought on the same day, but that it began sometime, I think, on the 16th or the 17th, as far as I can remember, of July, and then it went on for a number of days. As the Zvornik Brigade was capturing a certain number of prisoners during combat, then members of their military police unit were taking custody of them. I would like to note the following as well: Both of these senior officers were good and professional officers, commanding officers. However, they both had a kind of tendency of immoderate ambition to get promoted quickly. So this is also one of the ways they did that, through reports in which they stated that they were making major efforts, sustaining major casualties, in order to make the superiors believe -- or get a better impression of them about their professional capabilities. I have no reason, or any personal reason, to negate it, even if the unit did take part. I mean, it's a combat assignment. It didn't participate in anything that was illegal. But I know for a fact that it wasn't the way it was presented, so I would like to state that for my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In view of the fact that this is a question regarding the report on the combat readiness dated the 29th of November and that the report speaks about legal military activities, it does not speak about prisoners at all, then I don't know on what basis Mr. Vanderpuye is claiming that it took part in the capture and escorting of the prisoners which it captured and brought them to Batkovic, because in the third paragraph it already says that the corridor was open and that 5.000 Muslims had passed through. That is why I ask that the third paragraph also be read out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just bear with me for one moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. President. Two things. First, that's not what I'm claiming. I'm not quite sure what General Tolimir -- what his objection is. It's not my claim that the people that are mentioned in here are gathering prisoners or not gathering prisoners. It's the witness's testimony that's at issue, and the witness has testified, I think, relatively clear and on that. If General Tolimir feels the need, upon leave of the Court, to re-cross-examine this witness on that issue, then it's up to him to make that application and up to the Court to determine whether or not it's appropriate in the circumstances. But I think the record is clear as to our position and it's clear as to what the witness has testified to. There should be no mixing of the two. I would like to show the witness, first, P1459. We'll need to go to page 76 in the B/C/S first, and 77 in the English, and then we'll need to go to page 80 and 81 respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First I state that I didn't interpret the comment of Mr. Tolimir as an objection to a specific question, but it was more a suggestion to conduct the re-examination in a different way. But this should be decided by the Prosecution. I would like to ask Mr. Vanderpuye: What about the last document, 65 ter 7332? Are you tendering it? It just disappeared from the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just a minute. I'm sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was the last document you used with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I am tendering it. We intend to complete the translation of it, is the issue, so I guess it will be marked for identification, pending the completion of the translation. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. The document, 65 ter 7332, will be marked for identification, pending completion of translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I'd like to have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter document 7332 shall be assigned Exhibit P2184, marked for identification, pending full translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could I put up, instead, 65 ter 7337. And I'd like to have the witness handed the original of this book. It's the duty operations book for the Command of the East Bosnia Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, it may be given to the witness, with the assistance of the Court Usher. Mr. Vanderpuye, you should direct the Court Usher and the witness to a specific part of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I appreciate that. I just see that the translation I have up here does not correspond to the original, so maybe we'll have to do it on the ELMO if we've got one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The ELMO is available.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. If we could put the book on the ELMO, and we can go to ERN page ending 0528.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: With the assistance of the Court Usher, indeed. We don't see anything. Oh, it's not directed to the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Mr. President, I understand from Ms. Stewart that it is loaded and it's page 773 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was told it is in e-court, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- we don't need the ELMO anymore. The book should be taken away from the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm going to refer you -- if you want to hold on to that book so you can read it better, or if you need it in order to read what's -- what's written better, maybe you can take a look at it that way. But I'm going to direct you specifically to the entry beginning at 0500 hours. If you look beneath that, you'll see an entry at 1020. It's the second one from the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which date?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You should see on there that it should be the 15th of July, because a couple of pages forward, or the next page forward, you'll see the date of 16 July. But let me refer you first to this entry at 1020, where it reads: "They called from the Main Staff and ordered us to work pursuant to the order of General Miletic." At 1050, it says: "General Miletic - round up the men and send them to Pandurevic in the Drina Corps."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is it possible to enlarge it? There's a technical problem again, I think. And in English, is it possible to enlarge it? Thank you very much. And in B/C/S, it's not possible, I think. Oh, now it works. Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And then it says -- we can't see it on the screen, but you can on the book. In the column to the right, the second-to-last column in the right, it says: "Message received." And it's signed by somebody. And then: "Measures taken," in the last column on the right. And it says: "Inform commander of the East Bosnia Corps and the chief." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking about entries for 1020 and 1050?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's right. Let's go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is there a question or should I just follow the text?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just follow for a moment, and I'll ask you a question in a moment. We see entries here on this page, and I want to direct your attention to 1120 through 1820. There, in the middle of the page, you see the date, "16 July 1995." At the entry at 1110, it says: "Colonel Gengo - inform General Miletic that General Simic said that he cannot send the men to the Drina Corps." You'll then see the entry at 1820, which says: "General Gavric ordered 50 policemen to go to Zvornik ..." And then it says: "... 16 July 1995, and the unit commander to receive the task on 15 July 1995 in the evening." Can you tell us about these entries and the sending of police to the Zvornik Brigade, as referred to in this duty operations log-book for the corps command?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say this with full authority: This information has nothing to do with what I was talking about. This is the Chief of Staff, deputy commander of the corps, probably acted as commander of the corps in the absence of the commander. He ordered, along the military chain of command, that a part of the Military Police Battalion be used in a certain way, and sent them to carry out an assignment in the area of another unit. This entry has nothing to do, I repeat, with the assignment of taking custody of and bringing prisoners of war, about which I discussed in Belgrade and on the third floor with you and here in the courtroom. I followed this diary. The Main Staff asked for assistance and support. General Simic first said it was not possible, they couldn't do it. And then I suppose he changed his mind and his decision because the circumstances had probably changed, and they decided to send 50 policemen, who reported eventually to the Zvornik Brigade, and that's the assignment that I talked about. But I was confused at the time because I thought it was the same thing as the task that I testified about. This assignment, in fact, is completely different and separate from the assignment of bringing in prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's a different assignment. Is it different men?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a completely different assignment. A military police unit in this assignment did not carry out military police work. It acted, instead, as a regular combat unit in carrying out a task given them by the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, when they reported to him that they were joining their unit for a specific purpose. These 50 policemen reported to the commander of the Zvornik Brigade. From that moment on, until the moment when they returned to their original unit, everything they did, they did on the orders of the Zvornik Brigade commander, and the Zvornik Brigade commander was responsible for all their actions. But when I discussed something earlier, I discussed something quite different, the 50 policemen who went -- who drove in their vehicles to bring in prisoners of war to the Batkovic site. Now I see from this diary that there was also this particular assignment, just as many other assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: These are the same men?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were members of the same unit. They were not the same individuals. The Military Police Battalion numbered 200 to 300 people. You can look it up in the combat report, the strength. These 50 men mentioned here have nothing in common with what I talked about earlier. These 50 men went to another location to carry out a combat assignment. I talked about a reinforced squad who drove in their own vehicles to take custody and bring in the members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina who had been taken prisoner. They are not necessarily the same individuals by name, but they are members of the same unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So how many military policemen did the East Bosnia Corps have deployed to the Zvornik Brigade area in the Drina Corps on 15 July; a hundred? 16 July, I'm sorry. A hundred?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 15th -- or, rather, the 16th, under one assignment received from the commander or the deputy commander, 50 men were sent to the Zvornik Brigade, led by their commanding officer. They were told to report to the commander of the Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade to carry whatever assignments they are given by the Zvornik Brigade commander, and I did not talk about that assignment. I was not even aware of it until this moment. Or, rather, I was probably aware of it at the time, but it was not the focus of my attention in this case. During those days, another group of members of the Military Police Battalion, 10 to 15 of them, not more, would go every day whenever they were summoned by the Zvornik Brigade and told that there were 15 or 17, as we saw yesterday in the report of the commander of the Zvornik Brigade - I believe he mentioned that in the course of the day, he had 34 prisoners of war - well, these prisoners of war were taken over by those members of the Military Police Battalion and escorted to Batkovic. They were from the same Military Police Battalion of the East Bosnia Corps, but these 50 men were not on the same assignment. They were sent to the Zvornik Brigade and re-subordinated to the Zvornik Brigade; whereas the other group, the 15 men, carried out a completely different task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Vanderpuye asked Mr. Todorovic a moment ago about the people dispatched on the 15th. However, we see, in this column or paragraph 18, that the commander received them. However, in the Todorovic statement, we see that the take-over of prisoners was agreed on the 16th. This makes it obvious that these were two different and separate assignments, and I believe the Trial Chamber should take that into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the Trial Chamber will take everything into account, what we hear in the courtroom. I would like to put a question to the witness. You stated, and please correct me if that is wrong, that the men for these different tasks were from the same unit. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Other units of the military police in the Eastern Bosnia Corps, no, there were no other units; there was only this military police battalion. It had one APC Company, although it had no APCs, so it was practically a motorised company; then there was a traffic police; and then there was a company for logistics, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was not my question. I asked you about the two groups of 50 military police each. You said, and this is page 18, lines 16, 17, and 18: "These 50 men mentioned here have nothing in common with what I talked about earlier. These 50 men went to another location to carry out a combat assignment." How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe there's some misunderstanding due to interpretation. I've been trying to say that up to this moment, I was not able to remember, and maybe I didn't even know at the time because it was not my duty to know what orders the commander had given to whom. It is the commander who issues orders to the military police, not the security chief. These military policemen who were sent to the Zvornik Brigade were sent to help the Zvornik Brigade carry out their combat assignments. And until I saw this entry in this log-book, I didn't, perhaps, even know about it. What I knew about and conveyed to the commander of the Military Police Battalion one of those dates - I can't remember the exact date - is that he should send to the Zvornik Brigade one squad, that is, 10 to 15 military policemen, with the required number of vehicles, in order to take custody of and bring back ABiH prisoners of war to Batkovic. These 50 men are on -- are from the same unit, but they were not on the same assignment as the squad I just mentioned. Maybe these 15 men set out only on the 17th, whereas the other ones left on the 15th, and these 15 men make the trip several times over several days, picking up varying numbers of POWs each time. We saw yesterday that the total number was 171. Their task was to drive there, collect, and bring back the captured members of the BH Army to Batkovic, to the collection centre. Did I make myself clear now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You told me two times, or Mr. Vanderpuye two times, that you didn't know anything about the 50 policemen and their task, and again now, during your answer, you said: "Until I saw this entry in this log-book, I didn't, perhaps, even know about it." How can you conclude that these men had a different task than bringing in prisoners of war? How can you be sure of that? You stated twice that you didn't know anything about this different task to take part in combat activities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I keep saying I didn't know. But seeing this now in this diary, I'm trying to remember. And let me remind you that there has been a lot of discussion in this courtroom about who commanded the Military Police Battalion. The Military Police Battalion, as well as all other units, are commanded by the commander and perhaps the deputy commander in the commander's absence. In this case, the order was given by the Chief of Staff of the East Bosnia Corps, Galic. My superior commander is not required to inform me about what he decided and what orders he had given. However, concerning the 15th, he ordered me to pass the message on to the military police commander to designate 15 of his men who would go, more than once, to the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade to bring back groups of prisoners of war. Is it any clearer now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is a conclusion you are drawing today, is that correct, because you told us that you didn't know about the other task?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm stating with full responsibility now that this is the first time that I'm seeing this. Thousands of assignments during those few years were given to the battalion commander. The corps commander didn't ask me about that. He didn't have any need to ask me about that, especially in urgent situations when there isn't enough time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just wanted to know if this is a conclusion you're drawing today, because you said you didn't know about this combat task before today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. One additional question. You referred to a required number of vehicles to transport the prisoners of war. What kind of vehicles were used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Military Police Battalion had transporter trucks used for the transport of their own members and, if needed, for other persons too, because these are tarpaulin-covered trucks and they have benches at the back for sitting. These are transport trucks, and they are built specially for military purposes. They have broader, stronger tyres and other special features.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How many people could sit on such a truck? How many seats were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a rule, you can transport 22 persons at the back of the truck who are not carrying full combat equipment. If they are fully kitted out, then it can accommodate 10 per bench on each side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, you wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would perhaps like to make a suggestion to Mr. Vanderpuye just to ask Mr. Todorovic who was performing the escort duties. Would it be a traffic or transport unit? And I think he mentioned before that it would be the transport unit members who were conducting the transport of these prisoners because they were specifically not equipped for combat. So perhaps he could put that question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, you may continue as you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You heard General Tolimir's question, Colonel. If you're able to answer it, why don't you give him an answer.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's up to the commander of the battalion, when he gets an assignment from his superior officer, when he evaluates the specific nature and the weight of the assignment, which part of the battalion units he would engage in order to execute this assignment. Of course, as for combat assignments, he would assign most frequently members from the 2nd Company, the armoured transporter company, which is specifically designed for combat action. The 1st Company is designed to provide security. This is the motorised company; they provide security for the commander, the escorts, the collection centres, when they need to bring somebody in, and so on and so forth. The transport platoon is entrusted with escorting military columns that are moving. In wartime conditions, however, due to the units not being staffed up to full strength, it's up to the commander himself to study the assignment and to decide which part of the unit he would engage for a specific assignment. So I really cannot answer any more specifically than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, Colonel: If your commander had ordered the Military Police Battalion, through its commander, to report to the Zvornik Brigade 50 men and also given you an order to instruct the Military Police Battalion commander to send a squad to the same area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade of 10 to 15 men, as you say, how many of those men would have come under the command and control, as it were, of the Zvornik Brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just these 50 would be subject to the command of the Zvornik Brigade, who were obliged, when they report to the zone, to report in, and then they are completely under the command jurisdiction of the commander of the Zvornik Brigade. These 10 to 15 that I'm talking about, however, they were not under the control of the Zvornik command at all. They report to a specific location where these prisoners of war are located, they take custody of them, they make a record of their names, and then, under escort, they go to the location where they are supposed to hand over these prisoners. In this case, this was the Batkovic Collection Centre. So only these 50 people are under the direct command of the Zvornik Brigade. I was a little bit confused. I'm sorry, I didn't really speak very nicely of Pandurevic and Vulin, in terms of their character. But my question is: How can these 10 to 15 people be of any use to them in their combat assignments, but actually neglecting to think of these other 50? So this is what I talked about. I ascribed that to them as being too ambitious and that they boasted too much, but actually, when I said that, it slipped my mind that there were these other 50 men too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If Vulin took the 10 to 15 people, the squad that you asked him to set aside to transport prisoners, out of those 50 men, how many would have to come under the command of the Zvornik Brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not take the 15 from that group of 50. That group was compact, or it should have been. He took from the barracks, perhaps on the 16th -- I don't remember when I received that assignment. From the men who were still available, he formed this group of 10 to 15 men for this assignment that I'm talking about. These 50 left on the 15th, in the evening, to carry out their assignment. Up until the assignment was carried out, they were under the command of the Zvornik Brigade, up until the time they returned to their home units.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay, I think I see the problem. If we could go to 65 ter 7337. That's the log-book. I don't know if you still have it in front of you. And let's take a look at the entry at 1820 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I take it, from your answer, that you're under the impression that those 50 men left on the 15th. If you're able to read it, can you read what it says at the entry at 1820 hours?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I was just explaining. General Gavric ordered -- General Gavric, let me clarify, is the deputy commander and, at the same time, Chief of Staff of the Eastern Bosnia Corps, a person who has the right, on behalf of the commander, in his absence, to issue orders. He ordered 50 policemen to go to the Zvornik Brigade on the 16th of July, 1995, 1995, and the unit commander received the task on the 15th of July, 1995, in the evening. So in the night between the 15th and the 16th of July, he was supposed to prepare the men, to assemble them, issue them with adequate weapons. And then, on the 16th, report up there to the Zvornik Brigade in order to carry out the assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So they would have reported to the Zvornik Brigade on the 16th of July, not the 15th, according to this entry?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, according to what is written here, because the 15th is the date that the assignment was received, and then it states that they should go to the Zvornik Brigade on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you what's reflected --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It states here, clearly, that the unit left on the 16th and that the commander of the unit went on the 15th, in the evening, to receive the assignment. He went to Pandurevic on the 15th. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, are you not testifying in this courtroom today. So you may think about that as you want, but now Mr. Vanderpuye is conducting his re-examination. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Colonel, let me ask you again: If Dragisa Vulin, to whom you relayed General Simic's order, was told to set aside a squad of 15 men of that 50 that were supposed to go on the 16th when you spoke to him, that would leave 35 men to report to the Zvornik Brigade Command, wouldn't it? It's simple math.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my previous answer, I said that that was not the way to look at that. So these 50, on the 15th, in the evening, received an assignment somewhere. I don't know if it was at the command post of the Eastern Bosnia Corps or at some other location. On the 16th, they went to carry out that assignment. And others from that same battalion who stayed back in the barracks, policemen, soldiers, perhaps on the 16th, in the afternoon, or the 17th - I don't remember the date - when I issued the order, so Vulin took 10 to 15 men from those who were left behind, prepared them, take a certain number of vehicles in order to carry out this part of the assignment of receiving, transporting, and accommodating the prisoners of war. And he did that within a few -- he did that over a few days, 20, 30, 50, until the figure of 171 that we referred to in the courtroom here yesterday was reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you P1459. And we're going to need to go first to page 76 in the B/C/S and 77 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What you have in front of you now is - hopefully, we'll have it - is a copy of the Zvornik Brigade's duty officer note-book. And we've stopped on this page because we can see the date here of 16th of July, 1995. You can see that in the B/C/S, I hope. That's right in the middle of the page and it's boxed in. Now I want to show you -- we'll go to --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you page 80 in the B/C/S and page 81 in the English, and I'm going to direct your attention to the entry at 1050 hours. The B/C/S is not yet there. And in your case, it should be right in the middle of the screen in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it: "1050, 35 soldiers sent from the IBK to the IKM." If this is what you're drawing my attention to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Indeed. It reads: "At 1050 hours, 35 soldiers from the East Bosnia Corps, IBK, were sent to the IKM," of the Zvornik Brigade. What happened to the other 15 soldiers, if you know, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can just assume and to try to explain my assumption to you. General Gavric ordered that 50 policemen be prepared. However, when Commander Vulin appeared in front of him at three-metre distance to receive the assignment, then there is the possibility that he said, General, sir, I do not have the possibility of preparing 50 combat-ready men, but I can perhaps prepare 30 to 35 men, maximum, by tomorrow, and then they can be available. And then when he was receiving this assignment, well, now we could draw the information from their statements, perhaps. I'm just speculating. But I'm not connecting this in any way to those 10 or 15 for the other assignments, because this type of assignment, of bringing in, securing, and handing over assignments, younger policemen were not used, the younger officers who were fit for combat assignments. Security and all these other activities of different kinds were tasks for which older men were engaged, those who could not really undergo strenuous physical efforts. When the assignment was received in the evening, Commander Vulin explained that he could not prepare 50, but 35, and that this was approved, and that he sent 35 who had reported to the IKM of the -- where the commander of the Zvornik Brigade was. I don't have another explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Wouldn't the most straightforward explanation be that of the 50 men that were going there on the 16th, 15 were set aside to do the task that you were directed to inform Komandir Vulin to carry out, and that's why they don't report to the IKM, because they're not under the command of the Zvornik Brigade commander, 15 of the 50, and 35 are?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot accept this possibility, either professionally or personally, because from the beginning I have been telling you that I received the assignment from the commander for those 10, 15 men and for that task. These 50 never went through my head anywhere, and their engagements, so adding up those two numbers, 35 and 10 to 15, is not feasible. The 35 that, in the final stage, appeared for the execution of the assignment is one group, and this is distinct from this other group of 10 to 15 who were entrusted with taking custody of, transporting, and handing over the prisoners in Batkovic. Well, perhaps you can accept my answer. I don't have any other answer, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What happened to the 15 of the 50, then? What were they doing in the Zvornik Brigade on the morning of the 16th if they weren't reporting to the IKM? Do you know what was going on the morning of the 16th, or that afternoon, in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade? Did you hear about that? What do you think these 15 were doing, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps what I said was not interpreted. I specifically said in my previous answer: The commander of the military police unit of the Eastern Bosnia Corps, on the 15th, in the evening, was there to receive an assignment from the Chief of Staff, most probably, General Gavric, and he was told at the time to prepare 50 policemen. I assume that he said, General, sir, I do not have 50 men at my disposal right now in order to carry out this assignment. I have the possibility to engage 35 military policemen. Then - and I'm assuming this; it's an assumption of mine and an attempt to explain - then General Gavric approved that and told him, Very well, send those 35 policemen as urgently as possible to report to the commander of the Zvornik Brigade tomorrow in order to carry out the assignment. I don't have any other logical answer or explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to ask you again: How do you know that Commander Vulin explained that he could not prepare 50, but only 35, men? Do you know that for a fact or is it an assumption?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I'm speaking too fast, so that everything is not being interpreted. My introduction, when I explained this the previous time, and now, is that I assume, and then I explained what I explained. I wasn't present when Vulin was receiving this assignment or when he said that he had 50 or didn't have 50, or 30, or anything else. So I'm only assuming that this could have happened while the process of the implementation of this task was taking place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is an assumption and a conclusion you are drawing today. Why can you exclude the other possibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Why can you exclude the other possibility? How is it possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All this time since I've seen this entry in the diary, up until this moment now, I am trying to recall whether perhaps the battalion commander, when I relayed the assignment to him from the corps commander to take custody and escort the prisoners from the Zvornik Light Brigade, told me that there was already a part of the unit up there at the Zvornik Brigade and that this would not be a problem. Then I would accept that the difference then would be this, between the 35 and 50. However, I remember that the battalion commander did not inform me about that part, but accepted the assignment without any comment at all. That's why I assume and am basing my assumption the way that I have explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Colonel, wouldn't that be explained if you simply got the order before the order came -- that you got the order from General Simic before the order came to send 50 men? Isn't that the most rational explanation for why Vulin didn't tell you that there were 50 guys already in Zvornik, because they weren't already in Zvornik and he hadn't received that order when you told him that he had to send a squad down there? Isn't that the most rational explanation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my opinion, no, and that's because of the following: Only after this 16th does the combat report of the Drina Corps mention the first group that was transferred to the Batkovic Collection Centre. This is not mentioned at all before the 16th or the 14th. So as much as I can, I'm trying to make logical connections and conclusions. I'm sorry, but I do know, in a manner, the structure and the manner of command and decision-making, and so I am making a conclusion based on the manner in which we were trained and in the way we worked. So only on the 17th, perhaps, or the 16th in the afternoon, the first group was probably there that was supposed to be transported to Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I see. And so there's no record of that group because they didn't report to the Command of the Zvornik Brigade; right, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There isn't a record in this particular diary for a million other assignments that were carried out as well. The only things that are recorded here are those things that went through the Duty Operations Centre. So when the commander is not present, or the Chief of Staff, the duty operations officer is there 24 hours a day at the Operations Centre, and he receives information, assignments, and orders, and conveys them to whoever they are meant for. Otherwise, orders are received directly, by mail, personally, for the commander or the chief, and then the duty operations officer would not have access to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think it's time for the break. I have a couple of documents I'd like to show the witness, so maybe we should pick up then, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the log-book is still in front of the witness, I think. The Defence should have a chance to look into it, and we would like to see it after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Absolutely. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We must have the first break now, and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it that the Defence had the chance to look into the log-book which is in front of the Chamber at the moment. Mr. Vanderpuye, I just would like to draw your attention to the matter of including documents into the 65 ter exhibit list. We used the document which is now marked for identification P2184. That was not in the 65 ter exhibit list, but we always have this little note: "With the leave of the Chamber." We would always like to have -- to address that to the Chamber, that this should be included to the 65 ter list. I just want to remind the Prosecution. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Colonel, you had a look yesterday at D228, which was a list of Muslims that were exchanged from the Batkovic Collection Centre. General Tolimir showed you that list. And there were entries on that list showing the dates of arrival of certain prisoners from the 18th of July. You remember seeing that yesterday and commenting on that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In fact, on that list, the earliest date that's reflected that anyone came that was exchanged, as is indicated, was the 18th of July, 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether the 18th of July is the earliest date for the first group that came to the collection centre of Batkovic or that it's the date of the exchange, the first exchange. Maybe I am not quite sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, we can -- I can show it to you. It's D228. We shouldn't broadcast it.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. One page is enough, of the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the first page of the list. I think it's page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the first page of the list. There's a cover page, but I meant the first page of the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We can do that.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can see. This list is chronologically divided. The first group of five men arrived at Batkovic on the 18th of July, so that's the first arrival of the first group of prisoners at Batkovic Collection Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I don't want to mislead you, but it's actually not chronologically divided. But you are right; the 18th July is the first date upon which this list records individuals as having arrived at the Batkovic Collection Centre. I can see that the pagination isn't the same, but you can see clearly the 18th of July reflected in numbers 1 through 5 here. On page 5 in the English, if we go to number 49 - if we can find that in the B/C/S, maybe it's two pages forward - we'll see that date again reflected. Page 3 in the B/C/S, and it should be page 4 in the English, I suppose. One page in advance. That's right. And page -- you can see line 49, lines 55, and lines 60 also record the 18th of July. And, of course, you would have noticed there's no sooner date than the 18th of July. And then if we go a little bit further on to page 6 in the English, and we're looking for items -- line numbers 100 through 102 in the B/C/S, page 5, you'll see, again, numbers 100 through 102 reflecting the date of the 18 July 1995. And then if we go to page 7, and, again, also there's no earlier date than the 18th of July. And if we go to page 7, number 133 to 138 -- I'm sorry, 6; 6 in the B/C/S. 133 through 138, again you will see 18 July 1995 is the earliest date reflected. The following page, 8, and it's the next page in the B/C/S also, numbers 157, 162, 163, 166, and 170 also reflect the 18th of July, 1995. So you're right, it's not chronological. To your knowledge, these people that arrived at the Batkovic Camp on the 18th of July, how did they get there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at these dates, I can say with even greater certainty, and I infer, that it's certainly not the same group, those 35 and 50 men, as opposed to those 15 men on the same assignment. Those 35 or 50 were on a combat assignment, whereas the 15 received instructions from me, originally issued by the commander of the corps, on the 17th or perhaps the morning of the 18th, and the instructions were to go and bring back the first group of POWs to Batkovic. So the first group that was picked up to be transferred to Batkovic was picked up on the 18th. In other words, that group of policemen went to the -- went there on the 18th for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Went where?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the assignment I was talking about, issued to me by the corps commander to be conveyed to the Military Police Battalion commander, was to prepare and designate a group of men from the Military Police Battalion, and I said roughly it was 10 to 15 men, with the required number of vehicles. And that part of the military police unit went to Zvornik, to the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade, only on the 18th and took over the first group of prisoners that they escorted to the collection centre of Batkovic. And when they were told that there is a new group of prisoners, they again drove there and brought them to Batkovic, and so on over the course of several days until the last day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And who did they take these prisoners over from?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From someone in the Zvornik Brigade. I can't answer that question, really. I don't know. From somebody who is responsible for that sort of work in the Zvornik Brigade. And the first time they got there, they established contact, on the 18th. I mean, that part of the unit of the military police from the East Bosnia Corps made contact with someone in the Zvornik Brigade and took over the first group on the 18th. They agreed the mode of take-over for the next groups, and they continued until the last hand-over. Now, who that person in the Zvornik Brigade responsible for the prisoners was, I don't know. I don't know where they were based, in which house, which village, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How do you reach that conclusion? I mean, how do you exclude the possibility that these people were otherwise brought to the Batkovic Camp directly, without the involvement of your unit or with the involvement of your unit?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean which part of the unit? You mean the 35?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How do you exclude that the people that you see in this list that arrived at the Batkovic Camp on the 18th of July, 1995, did not arrive there from someplace other than Zvornik, or through some other unit, or with the assistance of another unit and your unit? How do you exclude all those possibilities and say, affirmatively, that these are the individuals that your unit took over in the Zvornik Brigade pursuant to the order that you passed on to Dragisa Vulin?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm making that conclusion based on the fact that I passed on to Captain Vulin the order I received from the commander, and the knowledge that this assignment was carried out over a number of days, beginning with the 18th, and that information was sent, every time a new group of prisoners arrived at Batkovic, that these prisoners were interviewed and registered by the ICRC, and they were given the first packages by the ICRC, and they were informed of their rights and entitlements in the procedure that followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I want to show you 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Let me put a question to the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, Mr. President. I hadn't noticed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- just to that. You received the order from the commander and you conveyed this order to Captain Vulin; that's correct, yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What did you tell Captain Vulin, where he should pick up the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I summoned Captain Vulin and told him as follows: The corps commander has ordered that you prepare and send the required men -- the required number of policemen and vehicles for the transport of prisoners of war from the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade. They should report to the Command of the Zvornik Brigade to be informed of the exact location and all the necessary details to complete the assignment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You were not told by the commander what kind of prisoners and -- this was referred to and where they have been before they were picked up by Vulin and his men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The corps commander told me briefly this. I spoke to the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic, and he told me that they have a certain number of prisoners, members of the BH Army. They need to be taken over to be brought to the Batkovic Collection Centre. I didn't ask him where these men were from, Sarajevo or somewhere else, but I knew that they were in the combat area of the Zvornik Brigade. And that's how I defined the assignment to the battalion commander, that he should send the required number of vehicles, with the necessary security detail, to take over that group of prisoners, members of the BH Army, from the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade. The leader of these men should report to the Command of the Zvornik Brigade to agree about the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: These individuals that are logged in as having arrived at the Batkovic Camp on the 18th, were they injured in any way?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew nothing about their health status, and I cannot speak to that. It was the camp warden who was supposed to know these things because he reported about the conditions in the camp to his superiors, just as I reported to my superiors. Everyone reported along their line of work about the situation in the area of responsibility of the Eastern Bosnia Corps, and these daily briefings were attended regularly by the camp warden of Batkovic, who reported to the commander about the conditions in the camp, how many prisoners needed medical assistance, whether any exchange was planned, how many people were planned for the exchange, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, you would have known something about these prisoners, wouldn't you? Isn't your responsibility or one of your responsibilities to interview them and gain information to pass on to your superior, General Tolimir, along the security chain or intelligence chain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some of the members of my service, from the section that I commanded and managed, were involved in the first reception and interview of the captured members of the BH Army. I explained that to the Prosecutor during proofing as well. The job was to make sure that personal details are correctly recorded in the files, to avoid errors and mistakes concerning certain facts that needed to be recorded, to establish to which unit they had belonged and in which part of the theatre they had been captured, and if any one of them was willing to provide information about their unit, although they avoided that, most of them. For the most part, it was not possible to get any important information from them, and we did not insist. This entire procedure of reception and providing the necessary conditions was the duty of the warden of the collection centre and his personnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The question was: Did you receive this information obtained from the prisoners, and did you forward them to your superior? You didn't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received information about the number of arrivals and their structure, and I reported that up the chain along the security line and also the corps commander. And we also compared our information with the warden of the collection centre to see if there are any discrepancies. Now, from the security aspect, I did not have any particular observations. It was impossible to get any information relevant for security or intelligence, so there was no need for me to report about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, sir, are you saying you, as the chief of security and intelligence in your unit, you just received a list of prisoners and not the outcome of an interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say I was not aware of the outcome, but the outcome was such that there was nothing relevant to security and intelligence in there. These interviews did not yield any information pertinent to security and intelligence. You can imagine that those people were frightened, confused, fearing for their lives, that sometimes they found it hard to even say their name, let alone tell you something important that would require my further engagement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. On page 40, line 16, Mr. Vanderpuye asked Todorovic whether he had provided that information to his own superior, General Tolimir. Please, the witness should be asked, loud and clear, what kind of information he provided to his security superiors, whether he was required to provide information about the health status of prisoners or security information, whether he was at all required to inform me about the state of health of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you should be patient. I'm quite sure that Mr. Vanderpuye will continue asking the witness about these matters. Please carry on, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just in context, Colonel, in your position as the chief of security and intelligence in the East Bosnia Corps, you did receive information concerning prisoners that were brought to not only the Vanekov Mlin, but also that were brought to the Batkovic Camp or Prison; right? All kinds of information.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my previous answers, and that's why I was trying to be brief now, so the day before yesterday, yesterday, and today, I said in my testimony that if needed, we would -- my service that I led would bring, from time to time, somebody from the Batkovic Collection Centre for an interview to Vanek's Mlin in order that the other prisoners of war would not be present or be aware that this person was being interviewed, and to prevent them later asking him, Who did you speak to, What did you say? So this is a part of the customary procedure in such events. Then in the first interview, you don't really get any significant intelligence/security information. Later analysis of everything would bring us to the conclusion that, for example -- well, I don't need to read the names, but one of these persons named was the commander of a certain battalion. After four or five days, when the person rests, begins to function normally, settles in, then there is another informational interview with that person, again in a normal human atmosphere, Where was he, Why was he there, Does he want to help us, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't mean to interrupt you, but it's a pretty basic question. And you can tell us, yes, you receive all kinds of information, or, no, there's certain information you don't receive, but what I want to know, specifically, is: When a prisoner is brought to the camp, do you receive general information, the number of prisoners, the condition of prisoners, where they're housed, or how they're secured from the camp? Do you receive that general information?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I receive such information -- or, actually, I get such information and data from daily briefings at the corps command, when they are submitted by the warden of the collection centre. I am then -- I acquaint myself with all the information then, for example, that there are three persons who are ill, there are four others who have different kinds of problems, and so on and so forth. The purpose of this initial data-gathering by members of my service is not to generally process the prisoners, but it's just an attempt, in this first blitz contact, to see and, in a way, check whether the whole procedure would be respected and whether all the people will enter the centre and be registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you get any information -- with respect to the individuals that arrived at the camp that we saw on the list on 18 July 1995, did you get any information that they were wounded or they were injured or they were in need of any kind of medical attention? Did you get any of that information?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My organs, two or three of them who participated, depending on the number of persons that arrived, I did not get information of that nature, nor was it their goal to gather information of that kind about the general status and the problems of captured members. Then, I repeat, later, during the briefings, I would listen to the report of the warden of the collection centre, for purposes of being informed, who then actually did report that kind of data, because the objective and the assignment of my service was not general care and regulation of everything that had to do with the collection centre. That is the job of the warden of the collection centre, who is directly responsible for the situation and the overall work of the collection centre. Again, I emphasise --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch what the rest of the sentence was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You started the last sentence with the words: "Again, I emphasise ..." What did you emphasise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I replied -- in my answer, I described what they did and what was the goal of the members of the service that I was working in joining in the interview or the conversation. It was just to gather initial information and to be present to see if everyone would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I asked you to repeat the last sentence of your answer, not the whole answer, only the last sentence, because the interpreters didn't get that. And you said: "Again, I emphasise ..." But what -- how did you continue this sentence? If you don't recall, it doesn't matter. Mr. Vanderpuye could continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I emphasise, again, the main objective of members from my service participating was to gather initial information and observations and to be present so that they could have insight as to whether all those who had arrived were registered and had gone through the reception process and are accommodated at the collection centre, to avoid the situation where you would have 50 reporting at the gate and 49 being registered as inmates, with one person missing, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The order to pick up prisoners, did that include going to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did the individuals, that is, the Military Police Platoon, did they go to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my answer to one of the previous questions, and Mr. -- the Presiding Judge asked me to repeat, therefore, my testimony about transferring the commander of the military police to report to the command of the Zvornik Brigade, and from the AOR of the Zvornik Brigade, to take custody of, escort, and place into the Batkovic Collection Centre the captured members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I -- well, perhaps it happened that during the implementation of the assignment somebody at the Zvornik Brigade said, There are five of them at a different location, so there would be a need for you to go and pick them up. That is something that, for now, I don't have any information on. I don't have any knowledge of that until this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to show you 65 ter 1434.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I know it's a time-consuming exercise today, but there should be one time you should come to an end with your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. There are actually a couple of -- I'm really trying my best to move through this as quickly as possible, and I'm sure you can see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's appreciated. But just a second. This list, should it be broadcast or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should not be broadcast. Thank you. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What you have here, Colonel, is a list of persons to be transferred under guard, and it indicates the 3rd Battalion of the East Bosnia Corps, and it provides a list of 22 individuals. It says persons were escorted on 18 July 1995, at 1600 hours, with their personal belongings. Is the 3rd Battalion of the East Bosnia Corps, the military police unit, the unit that you've been speaking about?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So these are your MPs, the corps' MPs?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And from this document it appears that they picked up 22 individuals at the day -- on the day and at the time that's indicated in this document.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And these individuals they picked up from the 5th Military Police Battalion, and it says "Vlasenica" here. That would be the Drina Corps Military Police Battalion, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, I don't want to use up extra time, but I can tell you we've checked this list of 22 individuals, and this list corresponds to D228, which is what I just showed you before, containing some 170 individuals. And every one of these individuals is on that list, and there is no one on that list that arrived at the Batkovic Camp on 18 July 1995 that's not one of these 22 individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, Mr. President, and show the witness another document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Were you going to put a question to the witness about this list?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, do you confirm that it refers to the unit that's under the command of the Eastern Bosnia Corps; that is, the Military Police Battalion of that corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the 3rd Battalion of the Military Police of the East Bosnia Corps, because often this Index 3 is left out and you just write "IBK," but it's actually the same thing, because there is this -- does this page have any -- does this document have any more pages, or is it stamped or certified in any way?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It has more pages, and it's not stamped or certified.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, is there a question? Do you need a comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, I don't need a comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, and I'd like to show -- under seal, and I would like to show the witness another document.
