utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1434 shall be assigned Exhibit P2185, admitted under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you P2168. I think we have a handwritten version of this same document, so maybe if we can -- and it might be on the next page - I hope so - page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't know if you can read that any better, but what it says in the English, and maybe you can listen to the translation and confirm that that's what's written in the handwritten version of this document, is that it's from the Command of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade. The document number is 08-34/95, and in the typewritten version you can see the date reflected as 18 July 1995. It is directed to the Main Staff Security and Intelligence Sector and the Command of the Drina Corps, and it reads that: "On 18 July, at 1545, 22 wounded prisoners from the 28th Division were evacuated, with a police escort provided by the Drina Corps, from the Health Centre in Bratunac." You'll recall that the document I just showed you, with the list of 22, says they were escorted on 18 July at 1400. So my question to you is: The 18 -- the 22 individuals that show up at Batkovic on 18 July 1995 didn't come from the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade, did they?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The previous list for me is like a blank document. There is no signature that they were taken into custody or handed over to anybody. It's just a drafted list, and there is a remark of who did what. There's no signature or indication that this was actually carried out. You checked that these persons are listed as people who arrived at Batkovic, but not on the 18th, but probably at some later date. That 5th Battalion of the Drina Corps most probably -- well, I'm concluding this. I don't have any personal knowledge about that. So they most probably brought them to Zvornik. In Zvornik, they stated that they handed them over at 1600 hours. As for whether they did hand them over at 1600 hours or later is open to debate, but I don't have any knowledge of it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to -- well, this document is already in evidence, I see. What I'd like to do, since -- if it's possible, is to have P2185 - that's just the list and we shouldn't display that one - displayed against D228. And if we could just go to the first page of that list and the first page of -- third page of that list and the first page of -- and this list, I think we should be able to make a comparison. It's the second page of 228 and the first page of 2185. I think we might have to display it in English so the Trial Chamber can actually compare the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, it's fine with this list. We can see the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us, just by number reference, which of the names on the left, which is P2185, correspond to the names on the right, which is D228?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you find the identical name, please don't say the name, but just indicate the number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number 12 in the Serbo-Croatian version corresponds to the number - just one moment, please - 5 in the English version. I'm sorry. Number 5 in the English version. And he arrived at Batkovic on the 18th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Maybe in the interest of time we should find a different one --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 9 in the Serbian corresponds to number 1 in the English version, and he was also brought there on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to say this briefly: It's very difficult to compare the alphabetical list on the right-hand side with the other list which has names, last names, beginning with different letters of the alphabet. The other list only has names, last names, that begin with an

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The list shown to the witness was shown in alphabetical order, but now we're looking at the same list. One is in English and one is in the B/C/S. I don't know what the difference is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is absolutely correct. Your observation is correct, but there's no other way to compare. Please carry on, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. In the interest of time, I'll just put on the record that number 1 in the list on 228 corresponds to number 4 on 2185; number 2 corresponds to number 9 on 2185; number 3 corresponds to number 19 on 2185; number 4 corresponds to number 12 on 2185; and number 5 corresponds to number 10 on 2185.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Those are the five individuals listed on 228, which is the list General Tolimir showed you, all of whom arrived, as is indicated, on 18 July 1995 and all of whom appear on the list that is dated 18 July 1995, indicating that your Military Police Battalion received prisoners from the Drina Corps Military Police Battalion at 1400 hours on 18 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sixteen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sixteen. Thank you for the correction. That's all correct; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of this stands with the proviso that the list is not signed either by the person handing them over or accepting custody. We don't know that the assignment was entirely carried out on the 18th at 1600 hours or was, perhaps, a number of those persons handed over later. This is very difficult now, after such a long time and from the place where I am now, to determine. I was not there during either part of the process, so I'm unable to say anything about that. The location is not given for the hand-over. All it says is that they were handed over to the 3rd Police Battalion of the East Bosnia Corps. I don't know if they were handed over in Vlasici, Milici, Zvornik. So there is a broad area for all kinds of conclusions, and that is why I wouldn't want to burden my conscience with that, since I wasn't the one who was carrying out this assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me show you 65 ter 144.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I don't see this document on the list of exhibits to be used during redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You're right, Mr. President. It's on the list of my -- it was on my original exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. But, again, you should be aware of the time you are using.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is an 18 July combat report, interim combat report, from the Drina Corps Command. It is signed by General Krstic. In paragraph 2, or item 2, rather, of this document, we read, and we'll have to get the first page in English: "Our 1st Zvornik Brigade, reinforced by a company from the 16th Krajina Brigade, a company from the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, two East Bosnia Corps Military Police Platoons, and a platoon from the 1st Vlasenica Light Infantry Brigade, successfully repelled all enemy attacks from the front, carried out the blockading and combing of the terrain in the general sector of Crni Vrh, Pandurica, Krizevici, as well as fully secured the old and new Zvornik-Tuzla road." You see that, and it refers to two platoons from the East Bosnia Corps Military Police on the 18th of July engaged in, effectively, combat activities. Can you explain that, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's already explained. On the 16th of July, a unit of 35 soldiers reported. That's approximately two platoons. A full complement of a platoon of military police is 30 men. And since we decided, by analysing all this, that there were 50, those are two platoons of 18. This document was shown yesterday as well, and I said that it's some kind of bragging, over-statement, because I really had no information that those 35 military policemen were sent to the Zvornik Brigade, and those are the 35. So they were there from the 16th, when they reported, until I don't know which date, and during that time they were assisting the Zvornik Brigade in their combat tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, this document wasn't shown to you yesterday. And let me just add that this document is dated 18 July 1995, because you can see, from the first line, it says: "On 17 July 1995, the enemy was carried out low-intensity attacks." So it's clear that it's the 18th of July. And the document I showed you earlier was Vinko Pandurevic's interim combat report of 16 July 1995, two days before this, where he refers, in paragraph 2, to the assistance provided by your military police as part of a military police platoon, and not two military police platoons. So that's my question. Can you explain that, because I would assume, and I'm sure you would concur, that Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic knows the difference between part of a platoon and two platoons, as is indicated here by General Krstic, the corps commander, or are they both making it up and exaggerating?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have nothing special to say, except what I've already said. I think that those are the 35 military policemen who reported, around 10.00 on the 16th, to the commander of the Zvornik Brigade. Whoever drafted this, and it's certainly neither General Krstic or Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic, but an operative officer who drafts such things, and he can make mistakes or use clumsy language, just like I, talking to you, clumsily used civilian terms until General Tolimir told me that I should use proper military terminology. I have no other comment to offer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me just add one last thing, and that is: You can see to whom this combat report is addressed, and it's addressed here to the Main Staff. Does that tell you whether or not it's likely to be clumsy and unfortunate language that's being used by a corps commander to communicate a dire situation faced by one of his brigades? Is that what you did in the Eastern Bosnia Corps? That's how you reported to General Simic, sloppily and clumsily?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, please, you should not understand this as sloppy or clumsy reporting, that that's not the way I put it. I was -- I am, after all, a trained officer. But in my unit, and especially in those light units, we had mostly reservists who had not even graduated from the School for Reserve Officers, but took up their duties and did their best.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thanks, Colonel. You were shown yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. I don't think this 18 July combat report's admitted. I'd like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 144 shall be assigned Exhibit P2186. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You were shown yesterday, Colonel, a document by General Tolimir which was a report concerning the Dayton peace negotiations. You'll remember that. And it indicated that he was engaged in those affairs from the 1st of November to the 21st of November. He asked you about what you knew about his ability to be engaged in those affairs and also be available and performing his functions, and you opined, and this is at page 13118, line 17, through 13119, line 4 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would appreciate it if Mr. Vanderpuye gave me proper references, because I did not ask the witness about my own abilities and performance, as indicated in lines 1 to 6, page 56.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye gave a reference on the transcript, and we all remember that you were dealing with this, your participation in the Dayton Accords. Please carry on, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The question was: "Thank you. Since we've seen in the Dayton Agreement document that on the 1st of September I was in Dayton, until the 21st -- actually, from the 1st until the 21st of November, could you please tell us, for the purposes of the transcript, could I have been both in Republika Srpska and in Dayton from the 1st to the 21st of November? "Actually," it says, "could the transcript reflect correctly your answer, since you've already gave an answer. So could the transcript correctly reflect whether you said yes or no. Thank you." That was the question. Your answer was: "My answer is that you could not have been in the Republika Srpska or in the Main Staff, performing your duty by establishment. Also, I can state with full responsibility that for a considerable amount of time before that period you had to have been absent from your duties in order to adequately prepare for such a complex and big assignment." I'd like to show you P1427. You'll recall that the Presiding Judge asked you specifically what information you had about the whereabouts of General Tolimir on the 5th of September, 1995, and that was in relation to the transfer from the Vanekov Mlin prison of Avdo Palic. I think we're going to need to go -- what I'm showing you now is a diary of General Mladic. It's admitted in evidence in this case. And I'm going to ask you to go to page 17 in the B/C/S. It should be page 7 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. We have is a -- I think, a transcript on the right of the B/C/S, and what I need is the English translation, if you have it. Otherwise, I can just have him read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And here we have an indication. It says: "Mali Zvornik, 1st September 1995 at 1500 hours." It says: "Meeting with General Janvier." And it says: "Present: ZV with five members, General Perisic, Toso, Gvero, Kralj, and I." The Toso that's referred to in this document, is that General Tolimir, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were only two of us with the nickname Toso: I, as short for "Todorovic," and General Tolimir. I'm sure I did not attend that meeting. Now, is there anyone else called Toso?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let's go to page 11 in the English and page 21 in the B/C/S. This one is dated 4 September 1995. Pale is the location. And it indicates a meeting with SRK commanders. I'd like to take you to page 17 in the English and page 27 in the B/C/S, which follows on from this meeting. And here we see a reference to General Tolimir, in particular; and it reads: "Intentions of NATO forces - they will continue to threat and use force at given moments. They may carry out acts and provocation along the axis Kiseljak-Ilidza-Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Does that tell you where General Tolimir was on the 4th of September, 1995? Does that refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, when I was questioned by General Tolimir, I stated with full responsibility, although perhaps that did not make him happy, that I was unable to speak about the dates and locations where he was at different times, because he was not required to inform me of his whereabouts. From the 1st to the 21st, he was where he was, and I believe for some time before that. Whether that some time was 10 days or more or less, I don't know. It was the necessary preparation time. I did not state at any point that he was there at any specific time before, the 4th, the 5th, or any other date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You said again, "1st to the 21st." Which month are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] November, the Dayton negotiations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That means two months later after these entries here in the war diary of Mr. Mladic; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not two months. A month. Oh, yes, sorry, sorry, yes. Yes, there's also October. You're right, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I don't see the purpose of more questions to that matter. Indeed, you should come to an end of your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I raise this issue only because it appears that that is the position that's taken by the accused in this case. I believe we've asked for specific information if there was alibi that was going to be asserted in the case, and it appears that during the cross-examination this is an avenue that the accused pursued with this witness, and that's the reason why I think it's relevant. I think, on the other hand, you're right, and I don't want to belabour the point. And since this is already in evidence, I don't have any further questions on this matter. There's just a couple -- a couple of issues I think I can raise with him in the remaining time we have before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I hope very much. Mr. Tolimir, you wanted to raise a matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Vanderpuye referred to me and my position. I asked the witness yesterday whether you were -- whether he was aware of where I was. I didn't claim that I told him about my location or whereabouts. My point was whether I was aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand what you are saying, but everything is on the record. There's no need for further discussion. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You were shown a statement that was made by General Smith, and General Tolimir put some questions to you, and quoted it, in fact, stating that eventually Mladic gave permission to the ICRC to visit the prisoners. At that time, he was not concerned about the reports that the BSA had separated men and women in Srebrenica, as the ABiH did exactly the same when they captured large villages. And General Tolimir put the following question to you, and he said: "Did you know, through the media or in other ways, that General Ratko Mladic approved or allowed the ICRC to register all the prisoners of war in Srebrenica? Thank you." And your answer was: "I know from the media, as I said, from the footage that is constantly being replayed, and from looking at parts of the transport of the population from Srebrenica to the B&H Federation, that the buses and the trucks that were going mostly were transporting women. There was the odd man also among them. As for the records and the presence of certain institutions, I really couldn't say anything about that as precisely as I've been able to talk about matters in the East Bosnia Corps AOR. That was my responsibility." Now, I do have a document that I'd like to show you, but I think, in the interest of time, I'll just tell you that in the UN report, which is D122, concerning the fall of Srebrenica, at paragraph 409, the ICRC reported that it was only able to register 164 prisoners from Srebrenica and 44 from Zepa and were told that no other prisoners were being held and were accordingly shown a number of empty detention centres in the Bratunac area. And this is following the London meeting which occurred in the middle of July. Let me show you a document that did go to the East Bosnia Corps, which is 65 ter 4072A. Here, we can see this is a Main Staff Sector for Security and Intelligence document. It's dated 29 July 1995, and it says that it's directed to the attention of the security organ of the East Bosnia Corps. That would be you. It talks about the disarmament of the Zepa Brigade, the 1st Zepa Brigade. And if we can go to page 2 in the English. If we can go to page 2 in the English, and we can read where it says, in the second paragraph on the page - it should be paragraph 3 in the B/C/S - it says: "Continue combat operations in order to surround and destroy the 1st Zepa Brigade until the Muslims make the exchange and carry out the agreement from the 24th July related to their disarmament and surrender. Take all necessary measures to prevent them from leaving the encirclement." And then it says: "Do not register persons you capture before cessation of fire, and do not report them to international organisations. We are going to keep them for exchange in case the Muslim do not carry out the agreement or they manage to break through from the encirclement." You can see this document was directed to your attention. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you give an answer: Mr. Tolimir, but, please, if you have an objection, you may raise it, but don't comment on this question before we have received the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Yesterday, in the course of examination-in-chief and cross-examination, he was not asked about events in Zepa at all, but I do not mind him being shown and read reports. That has been done before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And now your answer, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the heading of this telegram, you can see that the 1st Krajina Corps and myself received this report only for our information, about what is going on in a certain section of the theatre of war. All the listed assignments do not relate to my area, nor am I asked to carry them out, so I have no comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Colonel. I would like to tender the document, if it's not already in evidence, and I don't think it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't think so. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and that --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 4072A shall be assigned Exhibit P2187. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this concludes my redirect examination. I appreciate your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, you will be pleased to hear that this concludes your examination here in this trial. Thank you very much that you were able to come here to provide us with your knowledge and recollection. It was a lengthy experience. Thank you for your patience. You may now return to your normal activities. The Chamber would like to thank you again. We will have our second break now, and we will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before the next witness is being brought in, I would like to raise a few matters. One was the log-book used by the Prosecution during re-examination, 65 ter 7337. We have seen the original log-book and a partial translation. This document was not tendered during the re-examination, and I don't know what you want to do with it. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honour Judge Mindua. Yes, that's why I was standing. We just forgot. And I've spoken to Mr. Gajic about it. It didn't have a 65 ter number, but he has no problem. So with your leave, we would offer 7337 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The whole log-book or only those parts attached with a translation into English?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It would probably be a good idea to do three pages on either side just for context, but, yeah, you probably have enough to read. I don't think you need the whole log-book, nor is it necessary to translate it. So three pages on either side should get the dates and the context and cover it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The pages with the entries used with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. President. And I don't have -- I'm not sure exactly what they are right now, but we can sort that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I hope the Prosecution, together with the Registry, will figure out which pages have been used. The document will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7337 shall be assigned Exhibit P2188, and, in particular, pages 73 and 74 in original. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to raise another concern, about the length of re-examination, in the absence of Mr. Vanderpuye, who is no longer with us this afternoon. I would like to invite the Prosecution to reconsider the use of Court time during the examination. Some of the questions put to the witness in redirect could have been put to the witness also earlier in examination-in-chief to enable the accused to put questions to these issues during his cross-examination. It was a quite lengthy and much longer re-examination than expected by the Prosecution, itself. Sometimes it depends on the kinds and the way a witness answers. This is just a general remark, and I would like to invite the Prosecution to reconsider their course of action. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. We understand, and I know that you understood we -- this witness came off, fundamentally, what he had said in his statement to us, which was somewhat surprising, and so we hustled around to find other materials to try to clarify these issues, which were, as you could tell, fundamental, when General Tolimir made that call. So this was a massive issue, and that's why that took a lot longer. And you could see the way he answered questions. So that was a surprise. There was no tactical anything going on or strategic anything going on in that regard. And I'm not suggesting there is, but that is, of course, possible in this adversarial system, and that's not something I will stand for in that regard. But I would also -- and we discussed this. As you know, there was a six-hour cross-examination based on topics that had mostly nothing to do with direct; chemical weapons and alibi, other things that Mr. Vanderpuye had ready to go for redirect and didn't get to because of your concern. So when you have a six-hour cross that has nothing to do with the direct, that's one of the reasons why we go longer. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I didn't want to discuss this specific witness and this specific case. It was more a general remark to take it into consideration. The third point I would like to raise before we start with the next witness: The Chamber would like to address the Prosecution with respect to the issue of time estimates for another witness. As you are aware, the Chamber has adopted a flexible approach with respect to time estimates provided by the Prosecution for its witnesses. The Chamber has now noticed the quite drastic change in the time estimate for the viva voce witness Manojlo Milovanovic, scheduled to testify in May. The original estimate for this witness was five hours for examination-in-chief. The main note is -- records the estimate of 16 hours. Could that be simply a typo or is it a reasonable extension of your time estimate? If not a typo, the Chamber is curious to know why there is such a drastic change from five to sixteen hours. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I will have to discuss this with Mr. Thayer, though it's my witness. And I know I was -- we've been -- we have discussed this, and there's been a question of whether or not we -- that the five hours was based on the possibility of 92 ter. But I do know, generally, that, as you've seen, we have under-estimated sometimes and gotten ourselves in trouble because of that. And as we have watched issues develop, and sometimes we're not able to get to certain issues with certain witnesses, and I know that documents are being put in the General Milovanovic pile that may have been in the General Obradovic file for various reasons, and that pile for General Milovanovic has gotten bigger, frankly, and so I know that that's one reason why the -- why it's been raised. But let me discuss that with Mr. Thayer and think about it some more. I haven't really gotten to the nuts and bolts of preparing him yet, and there will be a better time estimate once I get to that. But as you can imagine, as Chief of Staff, he's an important witness, and there have been steadily-accumulating issues that we see the general brings up, very rightfully so, and that you have questions about. So that has -- what's created the higher time. That is a lot of time and -- but I think it was a reflection of a more focussed look, and I will continue that focussed look to see if I can bring it down, because I don't want to spend that much time with him, frankly. But we'll have -- we'll give you what we think is the best estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There's no doubt that this is a -- will be a very important witness. We wanted to avoid a misunderstanding because of a typo. Now you explained the situation, and we all remember very well the situation with the Witness Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have to pause for a moment because the record is not working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now it's working again. Mr. McCloskey, your last words are missing on the record, but I think there is no need to repeat that. You see the essence of your submission was recorded correctly. And I just concluded, after your submission, that this witness will be a very important witness, for sure, but you are invited to recalculate your time estimate again. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And also, on a related point, we're, of course, always trying to give you the best estimates, but I still am -- would rather err on the side of lesser than more, frankly, just because when we give higher estimates, then our whole timing gets fouled up, and it's actually harder on the opposing party, because you've seen -- and earlier, and it messes up their timing. So we have always tried to get either on or, you know, below, which means we go over, and we need to do better on that. But that's our theory, just so you know that, is try to get it on or below so that we don't have these big estimates that constantly get under-estimated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber appreciates the efforts of both parties to give a correct and reliable estimate of the time to be used during examination. And we would like to continue with our flexible approach on that, but we have to look into the problem of an expeditious trial, as well as a fair trial. And as we just have finished with our hundredth witness, we know that we have still some time ahead. The next witness should be brought in, please, but we go into a private session to enable us and the witness to explain his wish to get protective measures. We didn't decide on that yet because we would like to inquire the correct reasons for that. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber is informed that there are two visitors in the public gallery related to this Tribunal, not from the outside world, and, therefore, the Chamber grants to open the blind before the window of the public gallery. There are only these two people present. That will not pose any risk on the witness. Sir, would you please rise, and would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable. Again, you should be aware of the fact that nobody outside this Tribunal will see your face. Mr. Elderkin is now putting questions to you. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, could I start, please, by asking you to say your full name.

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC
utterances.text: My name is Nesib Salic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What's your nationality, please?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And from what country?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC
utterances.text: Pripecak village, the local commune of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC
utterances.text: Driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, where were you living in 1995, the first half of the year?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC
utterances.text: I lived in my village, Pripecak, and I did not move in that period. I was there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Who were you living with?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC
utterances.text: With my father, my mother, and four sisters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, your father's name?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC
utterances.text: Jusuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What were the conditions at your family's home at that time? How many people were there? What were you all doing during that period in 1995?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC
utterances.text: Well, there were people from all over the place, from Visegrad, Srebrenica, Rogatica. So I wouldn't be able to tell you exactly how many and where they were from, but there were a lot of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And how were you occupying your time?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC
utterances.text: Well, I stayed at home. I didn't go anywhere, and my parents didn't allow me to go far from home. We moved between home and shelter, home and shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Where was this shelter that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC
utterances.text: Not far from our home. Five, six metres from our home.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And why were you moving to the shelter sometimes?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC
utterances.text: Because there was shelling/sniping that we were exposed to, so I had to stay close to our home. I wasn't allowed to go far.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did that shelling and sniping take place throughout the first half of 1995 or did it only happen during a certain period?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC
utterances.text: It didn't happen that often, because in the period when it was about to happen, the shelling and sniping were more frequent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You've referred to -- I heard in the English interpretation as "in the period it was about to happen." Are you describing there the period just before the fall of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC
utterances.text: Yes. For a while before that, that's a time when we went from home to a hill close by, and everyone, men, women, and children, gathered in that meadow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'll come to that period in more detail. But just to finish off asking you about your background: How were your parents occupied during this period, during the first half of 1995?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC
utterances.text: Yes. My father was there. We had cattle, and he was busy taking care of it. My mother was preparing food, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you remember if there was a hodja in Zepa in 1995?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can you remember now his name?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC
utterances.text: I think his name was Hajric. I can't remember his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know if anybody else was a hodja in Zepa in 1995?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC
utterances.text: No. Hajric is the only hodja I heard about, but I had no contacts with him. I only met the man once or twice in that couple of years I was there during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know if he performed religious functions?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC
utterances.text: Well, if there was a religious rite somewhere, I heard people saying that they needed to invite the hodja.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And how about funerals, for example?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC
utterances.text: Yes. The word I used was "djenaza," a Muslim funeral.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: So he would attend those events, would he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know if my learned friend Mr. Elderkin is following the transcript, but the word actually used was not exactly interpreted. The interpreter used the descriptive term. So to clarify the transcript, maybe we should ask the witness to explain what "djenaza" means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: That's certainly something I didn't catch. I don't know what word was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: So, sir, could you please describe to us what "djenaza" means?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC
utterances.text: "Djenaza" means "internment," "funeral," but it's for the Muslim community. The Catholics use different rites and have a different term for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to go now to July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Gajic is still struggling with this word. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it's not my problem. I think it's a problem with the transcript. The witness actually said that "djenaza" means "funeral." That's what I heard in my language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it's not too major an issue. Just carry on, Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, how old were you in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC
utterances.text: I was 15. I just had my 15th birthday on the 15 of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: So were you in the Muslim army at that time?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC
utterances.text: No. I mean, certainly not. I was a child, a boy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know of any boys of your age who were in the army at that time?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC
utterances.text: No, because my parents, my mother especially, did not let me go far from home anywhere, so I spent most of my time at home, around my mother. So I had not much opportunity to go around and see if anyone my age was joining the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you remember the time in July 1995 when you learnt that Srebrenica had fallen?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of it then, but there was talk. When neighbours came to visit my parents, they would mention that Srebrenica had fallen and we had to run to the mountains, that hill that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: It could be a good time to break, Your Honours, unless we have any additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, it is unfortunate that we have a long weekend ahead. We must adjourn for the day. That means we continue your examination on Tuesday next week. The Court Usher will assist you during these days. We sat this week with two Judges, who are present today. Next week, we are sitting also with two Judges, but different Judges. Judge Nyambe will be back, and Judge Mindua has another appointment next week, so that we have the three days next week sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis again. We adjourn, and resume on Tuesday, 2.15, in Courtroom I. I wish everybody a pleasant and good Easter. We adjourn.
